prize_parts.citation: For an oeuvre that renews lyric, essay and narrative through an exacting dialogue between classical antiquity and modern experience, inventing hybrid forms in which loss, desire and the limits of translation take new shape.

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed. I still prefer Anne Carson (B002) as the single laureate, with Cărtărescu (B042) and then Zurita (B005) as alternatives. Round 1 produced no argument that moved me, and it did sharpen what the case has to show. The round-1 agreement on Carson is not a literary argument, and I do not use it as one. The case rests on three things in the work. First, the voice is recognisable in a few lines: cool, compressed, abrupt, and exposed in feeling. Second, form carries meaning. In Autobiography of Red the verse-novel structure lets the Geryon myth become a modern love story. In Nox the translation, philological commentary and archival fragments are the means by which the elegy mourns, and they are not set beside it. Third, the same preoccupations (loss, desire, the weight of the inherited past, the limits of translation) run through the poetry, the essays, the verse drama and the Greek versions, so the oeuvre reads as one project. On the chair's question about later work, my knowledge is general and public. I understand that Red Doc> returns to Geryon, and that Norma Jeane Baker of Troy and the later boxed and performance-linked books continue the experiments with the book as object. I cannot say from verified reading whether these deepen the project or only extend a settled manner. I therefore do not count the late phase as a proven strength, and I do not count it as a defect. The achievement I can actually defend is the core of original writing from roughly the late 1990s to the 2000s, and the citation should be limited to what that core supports. I also accept that the 'ideal direction' criterion points to imaginative and intellectual depth that gives literature new possibilities, and I read Carson's hybrid practice as meeting it. I treat that reading as contestable.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still sustained weight. Much of the work is short, fragmentary or object-like, and some of its effect depends on typography, layout and allusion that public descriptions cannot convey. If a close reading showed that the later books mostly repeat the gesture of the earlier ones, the case for the whole oeuvre would weaken and Cărtărescu, whose late phase including Solenoid reads as an extension of his materials, would be the stronger claim. A second objection is that the line between literary achievement and classical scholarship cannot be drawn cleanly. A third is that Carson can be assessed in the original English while Cărtărescu and Zurita are met mainly in translation, which risks letting corpus familiarity stand in for merit. I have to guard against that in my own judgment.

responses.point: Mattson says the case for sustained quality must rest on consistent invention across many small and medium forms, since Carson has no monumental work. She says that if later work does not show continuing invention, that should count against Carson and be stated openly, and she reads repeated reinvention of the book as development and not only a stable manner.
responses.response: I accept your condition, and I would answer the chair's question the way you frame it. If continuing invention in the later books cannot be established, the committee should say so and not assume it. My own account is thin there: I know Red Doc> and the later book-object works only from public descriptions. I can't say whether repeated reinvention of the book is development, as you read it, or a refined method, as I fear it might be. For that reason I rest the citation on the original writing I can describe with some confidence and avoid wording that claims a late phase. I also disagree slightly with how you weigh scale. Lack of monumental structure counts less against Carson than lack of evidence of deepening would. The first is a difference of form. The second would be an actual defect in maturity. If the committee cannot show deepening, I would move toward Cărtărescu and not simply lower Carson.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says that in Nox translation is itself the elegiac method, so it cannot be treated simply as secondary, and he frames the citation around the encounter between antiquity and modern experience and not around genre. He also names Cărtărescu's Solenoid as the best argument for placing him first.
responses.response: Your point about Nox answers the chair's question on scope better than my earlier wording did. I would credit Nox as original writing in which translation is embedded as method, and I would not credit Carson's translations as a separate achievement. That keeps the line you say is hard to draw and still lets the citation rest on her own books. I have adopted your framing around antiquity and modern experience in my citation, and I add the hybrid forms so that the wording is not read as a prize for classical learning alone. On Solenoid, I agree it is the strongest evidence of late ambition among the alternatives. That is why Cărtărescu stays my first alternative. Where I stay with Carson is that a late phase in Cărtărescu that expands his earlier materials is a maturity argument, but it is not yet a reason to put him ahead of an oeuvre whose formal reinvention I can assess more directly, and I treat that last point as an evidence limit and not as merit.

responses.point: Sward argues that sustained quality is not the same as volume: a consistent project with recurring concerns and visible formal development across decades can show depth without long books. She also says Carson's English can be assessed directly, which she treats as a point about evidence and not about merit, and she asks that the citation name the seriousness about grief, desire and inheritance.
responses.response: I agree with your first point and I have used it in my own weighing. I would add a limit to it: 'visible formal development' is the thing that has to be shown, and it is the thing the committee's reading is thinnest on, so the argument holds only if the development can be demonstrated. On evidence access, I agree it is not merit. I would go one step further and say we should discount for it explicitly. A candidate we read in the original has no hidden translation loss, and a candidate we read in translation may be understated, so uncertainty about Cărtărescu's Romanian prose or Zurita's Spanish should keep them as live alternatives and not push them aside. I also take up your request about the citation. My wording names loss, desire and the limits of translation so that the credit does not read as erudition alone.

responses.point: Olsson treats it as open whether sustained achievement is better shown by cumulative scale, as in Cărtărescu and Zurita, or by repeated formal renewal, as in Carson. He says an agreed citation text matters more than a rank because it fixes what is being credited, and he asks colleagues who know the Greek and English texts best to say whether the poems work for a reader without the sources.
responses.response: I agree that the citation text is the right place to settle this, and I have written mine to name original lyric, essay and narrative as the credited core. On your request about the Greek, I cannot claim philological expertise. I can only say that the Geryon story in Autobiography of Red and the elegy in Nox are legible as modern love narrative and as grief without the source texts, as I understand them from public descriptions. That is a claim about readability, not a verified finding, and a colleague who knows the Greek better should test it. On scale versus renewal, I remain with renewal for now, but I would not call the question closed. I see no way to decide it from the evidence in these files, and I would not let a count of earlier rankings stand in for that decision.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's most recent decade of work deepens the project or refines an established method is not something I can verify. My knowledge of later titles such as Red Doc> and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy is general and unverified.

How much of the effect of Nox and similar works depends on typography, layout and physical form, which cannot be fully assessed from public descriptions and may carry unevenly into Swedish and other languages.

Where the line falls between original literary achievement and classical scholarship or translation, and whether Nox should count as original writing with translation as method, remains a judgment for the committee.
I have not independently verified any text or the full corpus, and the shortlist gives only two representative works per writer, so every whole-oeuvre claim rests on general public knowledge.

Whether a close reading of Cărtărescu in Romanian or Zurita in Spanish would change the order cannot be settled from translations, and the difference in evidence access between Carson and the alternatives is a limit on this comparison and not a point about merit.
Whether the committee reads a hybrid scholar-poet practice as meeting the 'ideal direction' criterion is unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which lists no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to Anne Carson or to any other shortlisted writer. The profile records my own interests in ekphrasis, myth and fairy tale and my Lagerlöf biography. These are context about my own practice, not evidence of a preference or a ground for recusal. Ingrid Carlberg is a co-opted member whose actual voting status is undocumented, so her simulated vote is a modeling assumption. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
